clue.text: In wild orgy I torment mathematical science

indicators.note: wild suggests letters running out of control into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone tormented by a wild party confesses it to a maths subject.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wild' rearranges ORGY, I and TORMENT, twelve letters exactly.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the branch of mathematics dealing with triangles, angles and their ratios, so a mathematical science.

clue.text: Proposition for article to get more confused…

parts.note: the definite article

indicators.note: confused tells us the letters of the word more are muddled up

explanation.surface: A proposal put in an article only makes things more muddled.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis carries the surface on into 2 Down; 'to get' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A proposition proved from axioms in mathematics or logic is called by this name.

clue.text: … in certain dialogues of state

indicators.note: in says the letters sit inside the words certain dialogues

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: a statement found in certain philosophical dialogues.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis links it to 1 Down's surface. 'in' marks the letters inside certaIN DIAlogues.
explanation.definitionFit: A nation, here the large country of South Asia, is a state.

clue.text: Variation of airs too, or songs in these works

indicators.note: a variation of something is a changed version, so the following letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Composers vary airs in large choral works.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Variation of' rearranges AIRS, TOO and OR.
explanation.definitionFit: These are large-scale musical compositions for voices and orchestra, typically on sacred themes, made up of arias and choruses.

clue.text: No old tanner but an exiled poet

parts.note: no means nothing, zero, the letter O
a tanner was the old British sixpence, written VI D (six pence, D for the old penny)

explanation.surface: Not a former leather-worker but a poet sent into exile.
explanation.walkthrough: A tanner was British slang for the pre-decimal sixpence; D stood for pence, so six pence is VI D.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman poet of the Metamorphoses was banished by Augustus to Tomis on the Black Sea.

clue.text: Contrive to 'appear English — in green perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps signals that the letters could be arranged otherwise

explanation.surface: Trying to look English by dressing in green.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges E with IN GREEN.
explanation.definitionFit: To engineer a result is to contrive or manoeuvre it into happening.

clue.text: "The chapter on the Fall of the you may omit" (Wilde)

definitions.text: "The chapter on the Fall of the you may omit" (Wilde)

parts.words: The chapter on the Fall of the you may omit
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation: Miss Prism's line in Wilde's The Importance of Being Earnest, set for Cecily's lessons on political economy, missing a currency's name

explanation.surface: A line from Wilde with one word left blank.
explanation.walkthrough: Miss Prism tells Cecily she may skip the chapter on the fall of the Indian currency as too sensational.
explanation.definitionFit: The Indian monetary unit, whose falling value was topical in Wilde's day, completes the quoted line.

clue.text: Prince reigning full of promise

parts.note: regnant is a formal word meaning reigning, as in a queen regnant

explanation.surface: A prince on the throne shows great promise.
explanation.definitionFit: A moment or pause heavy with significance or likely outcomes is described this way, like a promising situation.

clue.text: Irishman goes to church for a spiritual meeting

parts.note: Sean is a typical Irish man's name
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: An Irishman heads to church for a religious gathering.
explanation.definitionFit: A gathering where people try to contact spirits of the dead is a spiritualist meeting.

clue.text: Like Moore's young charms

parts.note: a quotation clue: Thomas Moore's song begins 'Believe me, if all those ... young charms', and the missing adjective fills the gap

explanation.surface: Describing the youthful attractions in a song by Thomas Moore.
explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Moore was an Irish poet; his song 'Believe Me, If All Those Endearing Young Charms' supplies the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Charming, lovable qualities that win affection are described with this adjective in Moore's famous lyric.

clue.text: Good beginning in simple removal of undesirables

indicators.note: in places that letter within the word for simple

parts.note: pure can mean simple, unmixed, as in pure and simple

indicators.note: the beginning of the word Good is its first letter

explanation.surface: A fresh start brought about by a simple clean-out of unwanted people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beginning' takes G from 'Good'; 'in' puts it inside PURE.
explanation.definitionFit: A political purge is a sweeping expulsion of people a regime considers disloyal.

clue.text: Argue about a child?

parts.note: re means about or concerning
a son is a male child

explanation.surface: A quarrel over a youngster.
explanation.definitionFit: To argue logically, working through a case, is to think things out with this verb.

clue.text: It's gone, Anne's poor figure

indicators.note: poor suggests the letters are in a bad state and must be reordered

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: Anne laments that her poor figure has gone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poor' rearranges GONE and ANNE; 'It's' is a link and the possessive adds no letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A plane shape with nine sides and angles is a geometrical figure.

clue.text: Failin' to catch what's for tea

definitions.meaning: to muff is to fail to hold a catch, and dropping the final g gives a colloquial form
a toasted bread roll served at afternoon tea

explanation.walkthrough: In Britain, 'tea' can be an afternoon snack or a light evening meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Muffing a catch is fumbling it, spoken with the g clipped; separately, a flat yeast cake is a classic British teatime food.

clue.text: Cape Company leads in stability

indicators.note: leads says the company word goes in front of the cape word

parts.note: a firm is a business company
a ness is a headland or cape, as in Loch Ness's neighbour Dungeness

explanation.surface: A coastal business takes the lead in providing stability.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue names the cape first, but 'leads' puts the company word in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Steadiness and solidity are the quality of being unmoving and stable.

clue.text: Set off for school in time

indicators.note: in places the school inside the time word

parts.note: a date is a point in time
Eton is the famous English public school

explanation.surface: Leaving for school on time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' is only a link; Eton is the famous English boarding school near Windsor.
explanation.definitionFit: To set off a bomb or charge is to make it explode.

clue.text: Gear to press too much ?

definitions.meaning: a gear in a car above top gear, for economical cruising
to drive someone too hard, overworking them

explanation.definitionFit: It names an extra-high gear ratio in a vehicle, and read as two words it means to drive or push someone beyond reason.

clue.text: Man of steel gives rise to confusion in drink

indicators.note: in puts the turned word inside the drink

parts.note: beer is a drink

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means reading from the bottom up, so the confusion word goes backwards

parts.note: a mess is a state of confusion

explanation.surface: Someone tough wakes up muddled after drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'gives rise to' turns MESS into SSEM, which 'in' puts into BEER.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Bessemer invented the process for mass-producing steel cheaply from pig iron.

clue.text: Will Scarlet, for instance, the author

definitions.meaning: one of Robin Hood's band, who lived in Sherwood Forest
C. S. ..., who wrote the Hornblower novels

explanation.walkthrough: Will Scarlet is one of Robin Hood's outlaws in English legend.
explanation.definitionFit: Robin Hood's merry men were woodland dwellers, and the novelist of the Hornblower naval stories bore this surname.

clue.text: Easy to find bill among the papers

indicators.note: among puts the bill inside the papers

parts.note: a file is a set of papers
AC, short for account, is a bill

explanation.surface: It's simple to locate an invoice in the documents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'among' puts AC into FILE as F-AC-ILE.
explanation.definitionFit: Facile means superficially easy, achieved without effort.

clue.text: It whirls a girl to the summit

parts.note: Peg is a girl's name, short for Margaret
the top is the summit

explanation.surface: A girl spins round on reaching the peak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A pear-shaped spinning toy with a metal point is wound with string and set whirling.

clue.text: Shut up about the parson stop!

indicators.note: about places the shut-up word around the parson

parts.note: pent, as in pent-up, means shut up or confined
Rev is short for Reverend, the title of a parson

explanation.surface: Someone yells at a preacher to be quiet and cease.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shut up' looks like a command but is the adjective meaning confined, as in pent-up.
explanation.definitionFit: To hinder something from happening is to stop it.

clue.text: As chalk is to cheese, this is

definitions.text: As chalk is to cheese, this is

parts.words: As chalk is to cheese, this is
parts.note: the phrase 'like chalk and cheese' describes two things utterly unlike each other

explanation.surface: Comparing chalk and cheese, the most unlike of things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As different as chalk and cheese' is a British idiom for complete opposites.
explanation.definitionFit: A striking difference between two things set side by side is what the idiom expresses.

clue.text: Is roughly speaking an artist's afterthought

parts.note: RA, a Royal Academician, is an artist; the possessive 's is kept as S
PS, a postscript, is an afterthought at the end of a letter

explanation.surface: Roughly speaking, a painter adds a postscript.
explanation.walkthrough: Here the 's of 'artist's' supplies a letter: RA'S then PS.
explanation.definitionFit: To rasp is to speak in a harsh grating voice, so the third-person verb says someone is talking roughly.

clue.text: A note instead of information

parts.note: D is a musical note
vice, as in vice-captain, means in place of

explanation.surface: A memo replacing some information.
explanation.definitionFit: In commerce, an advice is a formal notice or piece of information, such as a remittance advice.

clue.text: Get used to railwaymen? That's about it

indicators.note: about puts the that-is letters around the union

parts.note: i.e., id est, means that is
the NUR was the National Union of Railwaymen in Britain

explanation.surface: Asking whether one ever adapts to railway workers, and finding that's the gist.
explanation.walkthrough: The OCR dropped 'to'. The NUR was the old British rail union, merged into the RMT in 1990.
explanation.definitionFit: To accustom oneself to hardship until one no longer feels it is to become hardened.

clue.text: Vivacity of the French in two quarters'

indicators.note: in puts the French word between the two compass points

parts.note: E and N, east and north, are points of the compass, or quarters
la is the French feminine word for the

explanation.surface: French liveliness found in two districts.
explanation.walkthrough: Compass points are often 'quarters' in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: Flair, dash and spirit, a word borrowed from French, is vivacity.

clue.text: Endures certain loads

definitions.meaning: a last is an old unit of weight or cargo, varying by goods

explanation.definitionFit: Something that keeps going survives over time; a last was also an old measure of cargo, so the plural names certain loads.

clue.text: Many men the Prince of Arragon called "fool" and "barbarous"

definitions.text: Many men the Prince of Arragon called "fool" and "barbarous"

parts.words: Many men the Prince of Arragon called "fool" and "barbarous"
parts.note: in The Merchant of Venice, Arragon scorns the 'fool' crowd and 'barbarous' masses who choose by outward show

explanation.surface: A Shakespearean prince sneering at the common herd.
explanation.walkthrough: Arragon, choosing among Portia's caskets, refuses to rank himself with the common crowd.
explanation.definitionFit: The great mass of ordinary people, the crowd, is what Arragon disdains.

clue.text: Trent's menage sadly leads to alienation

indicators.note: sadly suggests the household is in a sorry, disordered state

parts.note: the name Trent with its possessive s, all used as letters

explanation.surface: Trent's household breaking down leads to a family split.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sadly' rearranges TRENTS and MENAGE; the possessive S is needed here.
explanation.definitionFit: Becoming distant or estranged from someone once close is alienation.
